These traditional approaches, however, often underperform in complex, real-world scenarios and have been difficult to enhance, in part, due to the lack of abundant, high-fidelity ground truth data. As its core, AS3 employs a scene-dependent spatial metric learned by a discriminator that classifies gradient-descent-optimized progressions as authentic. Concurrently training with both audio and text data has been shown to significantly enhance automatic speech recognition (ASR) performance, especially when extensive text annotations are available. To such an extent that current leading models often rely almost exclusively on this multi-modal approach for training.

However, existing methodologies tend to use fixed, uni-directional mechanisms for multi-modal pre-training. Our work introduces an innovative scheme for bi-directional attention during multi-modal training. By allowing text and audio features to interact through two self-trained attention mechanisms, the system simultaneously processes text from audio data and audio from text data. Here, "text from audio" is calculated by using audio data to extract the most relevant text from a knowledge base, and "text from audio" is accomplished through employing textual inputs to focus on particular areas within the speech audio data for recognition. We integrated this innovative training strategy into the end-to-end ASR system known as Content-based Attention Module (CAM).

Testing this design within the WeChat app showed that adding just this module improves text-based attention systems by an average of 0.5 absolute percentage point, with significant increases reported in challenges regarding complex natural language chat scenarios. This evidence supports the conclusion that minimal multi-modal enhancements can effectively improve ASR systems.

Our research investigates asymptotic properties of $\hat{\n}$, a random uniform parking function of dimension $n$. Recently, we reported on a novel gate-tuning mechanism for a conductive state in Niobium Nitride (NbN) nanowires, situated between two regimes of quantum phase slippage and coherent tunneling. Radiation constraints inherent to positron emission tomography (PET) imaging hinder its application for studying vulnerable groups such as pregnant women, children, adults needing frequent scans. While reducing radiation exposure is critical, it often results in reduced scan quality; although various strategies address this, they typically fail when encountering new data scenarios. Multidirectional learning with uncertainty awareness, using X-ray CT and MRI as guides, has demonstrated success in reducing doses for aligned modalities but remains effective only when new X-ray CT or MRI data strictly follow the distribution of the training set—conditions rarely met in practice since new configurations constantly emerge. Since a reduced-dose PET image effectively represents novel, unrelated out-of-distribution (OOD) data relative to concurrent X-ray CT or MRI, we propose redesigning the training paradigm so that learners recognize and respond to PET as genuine OOD input rather than forcing alignment. Specifically, we introduce a novel approach—uncertainty-aware multimodal learning with Voxel-deleveling Networks (VoxNfs), which forces modalities to match while preserving structural features. We argue that low-dose PET represents higher uncertainty compared to heavily cross-referenced X-ray CT or MRI. Testing on datasets containing paired low-dose PET and high-res MRI or CT confirms that our method significantly surpasses current approaches in reducing dose protocols, particularly when out-of-distribution low-dose PET data is involved, as measured by statistical uncertainty scores and visual quality checks.

Results from the MRDT dataset demonstrate both the flexibility of our system in producing different types of attention and the significant improvement in performance achieved through the proposed training method.

Smart wearable devices have the ability to collect detailed user health data, offering significant potential for early disease detection and prevention. However, their widespread adoption is hindered by concerns regarding privacy and data security. Federated learning (FL) offers a promising solution by keeping data on users' devices while still enabling model improvements through distributed training. To solve these issues, we introduce "FedHealth," a transfer knowledge framework built for wearables in healthcare. By integrating easy-entry wearable models and leveraging their established user bases, we allow a new device to benefit from knowledge that is relevant and specific to a user. Experiments conducted on two distinct wearable platforms demonstrate that our framework not only imparts useful capabilities to a new device but also results in more accurate and reliable health screenings than the best existing methods.

This work is a comprehensive, accessible guide to fundamental epidemic modeling mathematics. Written during the global COVID-19 crisis with immediate applicability in mind, the guide explores how these models tracked the new SARS-CoV-1 outbreak, offering an engaging narrative of the current epidemic intertwined with mathematical principles. Recently expanded with fresh data and insights from the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 event, it serves as a vital, up-to-date resource for students, researchers, and professionals in physics, natural and mathematical sciences, and public health.

We introduce Updates-DNA-Hybrid Tree (UDHT), a novel file system architecture designed to address current limitations in DNA storage solutions. While existing DNA storage systems offer terabyte capacity at petabyte scale with proven read and update models, they inherently lack robust hierarchical organization; prior designs flatten all files to equal priority, making it impossible to distinguish between critical and non-critical data. UDHT corrects this by introducing traditional tree hierarchies where users can classify files, updateability, and integrity checks, ensuring that essential data is stored as structured nodes while less important information remains attached. Furthermore, UDHT implements a distinct storage model for leaf and non-leaf nodes, respectively optimizing reads, writes, and updates against these constraints to achieve a balanced system. Evaluation results demonstrate that although updating hierarchically organized DNA data incurs some overhead compared to standard systems, the performance overhead averages 0.0005 of a day per update operation in practice – an amount too negligible to impact utility in favor of significantly improved storage management capabilities.

Probe data has emerged as a cost-effective alternative to traditional short-term volume estimation; however, most existing models depend on data that spans long periods. Numerical simulations of gravitational systems require solving partial differential equation constraints for initial data; if these are not satisfied, evolution fails. This work introduces a new algorithm utilizing the Coupled Triangular Factorization with Pivot (CTFP)—a technique previously applied to numerical integration of constraint Hamiltonians—to solve the Einstein constraints. Following orthogonalization of both momentum and Hamiltonian constraints, the method employs CTFP to resolve the momentum constraints prior to evolving variables. This sequence transforms the Einstein constraints into a new set that is equivalent to the original formulation but significantly easier to solve. Testing in flat space demonstrates that this new approach handles both linear and gravitational radiation. When compared against standard multigride methods in a numerically simulated collapsing black hole scenario containing linear perturbations, the CTFP-based strategy yields a solution of the same accuracy with roughly 15% less computation, an improvement that increases when simulating gravitational self-force is included.

To address these limitations, this paper presents Dynamic Graph Network (DGN), a recurrent neural architecture utilizing a dynamic network filter applied independently across each node to model input correlations with the rest of the network adaptively. Critical to DGN is its efficient design: it estimates directional connectivity with a single time step, offering immediate results that do not necessitate a warm-up phase. We validated DGN first on simulated data featuring known ground-truth connections, demonstrating its superior accuracy in recovering these patterns compared to traditional and current comparative approaches. Furthermore, testing with human electroencephalogram (EEEG) data revealed that DGN effectively detects directional connectivity states that align with distinct neurological states, reliably distinguishing them in practical applications.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) represent the cornerstone technology for solving various deep image recognition challenges; however, they remain susceptible to backdoor attacks, where an adversary injects a specific trigger into the training data to create a malicious trigger-backdoor model. This study introduces Global Mean Pooling (GMP) as a novel trigger design for such attacks. Unlike traditional triggers that rely on distinct patterns or added noise, GMP effectively functions despite the complete absence of any backdoor-specific component in the training images. Instead, it exploits the natural, bias-prone feature extraction of CNNs—specificing that certain semantic classes often consistently map to higher average activation values across global pooled outputs during training. Because these class-specific biases are inherent outcomes of the training process itself, using GMP as an undetectable trigger renders the resulting backdoor attack significantly harder to identify than those built around more anomalous triggers. Furthermore, since the attack operates purely within the standard training framework, it remains entirely compatible with existing methodologies for detecting triggers or manipulating training procedures to foil logic. Extensive experiments confirm that this attack not only evades current state-of-the-art detection mechanisms but also proves robust against robustness attacks and transferable to other model architectures.

High-precision astrometry relies on relativistic modeling, making it sensitive to uncertainties in the PPN parameter $\gamma$. Using a perturbation approach, we analyze parallax measurements from a standard Gaussian distribution of stellar positions and ellipses, positing that $\gamma$ deviates from its standard value of 1 according to a normal distribution. By deriving the conditional parallax for specific $\gamma$ realizations and averaging it, we obtain the expectation value and uncertainty intervals. Results indicate whether treating $\gamma$ as a stochastic variable significantly alters astrometric solutions; specifically, 50 % confidence intervals for $\gamma$ widen by a factor between 1.02 and 1.05 depending on baseline distance, while mean parallax values shift within [0.002;0.006] mm$^{-1}$ across the same baselines. Furthermore, the response varies non-unologically with distance: close to 100 nearest stars exhibit parallax errors nearly double what they would be if $\gamma$ were fixed, demonstrating maximum sensitivity for proximate objects regardless of total sample count. Finally, we suggest utilizing this probabilistic framework not only to quantify current Gaia limitations but also to optimize the design of future generations of astrometric missions.

Given a set of distributions where only specific parameters define their structural differences, this study introduces a generalized estimate for the "average" parameter distribution. For explicit Markovian chains restricted to a state subset or any univariate function derived from such chains, there exists always a corresponding family member containing average parameters. We provide constructive proof of existence for exponential family distributions and define general MLE estimates for these averages, enabling efficient Monte Carlo simulation through processes like Gibbs sampling. Using an i.i.d. statistical process, we demonstrate how these generalized MLE characteristics achieve convergent precision as sample sizes increase. Finally, we illustrate the practical applicability of these findings by examining generalized estimates specifically tied to von Misher-Laplace (vM-L) distributions.

Knowledge Tracing (KT) represents a series of methodologies designed to dynamically model a learner's proficiency based on an interactive training history, having attracted considerable attention within the education community. However, knowing which specific model to select for a distinct learning scenario remains challenging. While large-scale evaluations are standard for knowledge-graph based or traditional methods, deep learning-based KT models often rely on smaller, limited studies. To resolve this gap, we present pyKT—a web-enabled toolkit built on Python that facilitates the conduct of scalable knowledge tracing evaluations. We detail our framework by releasing two critical assets: first, the adaptation of several prominent deep learning-based KT models to the pyKT environment, and second, a suite of library functions crafted to manage the complexities of massive-scale experiments. We illustrate the utilities of pyKT through an experiment scaling to one trillion interactions over two diverse datasets. Additionally, we establish benchmark comparisons between two major modeling architectures and offer insights into evaluating next interaction predictions using a shared score, known as PyF1.

The team-based proof reporting method known as new format argument (TPT argument) has evolved significantly, with a wide range of SMT systems contributing new rules to the format, effectively creating an ad-hoc, distributed specification language. This study aims to design a general framework to define validating strategies for formula sets composed of TPT rules. Utilizing this approach, we successfully defined the verification procedure applicable to the combined logic used in the CAV theorem proving library. Consequently, our project extended this logic by incorporating rules from first-order logic, F-logic, abstraction rules, and bitscribe, ultimately establishing the logic found in the version 4 release (SMT). As part of the project, we also created a high-level, logic-generic representation for these rules and implemented an abstract solver using said framework; by translating translations of various solving procedures into generic form, we realized actual solvers capable of actually resolving problems using actual data.

Federative learning allows multiple participants with private data to jointly train a model. However, limitations like limited bandwidth and the desire for anonymity often result in federated updates being sent out of sync and added together in an unorganized way. Traditional methods using asynchronous and heterogeneous aggregation faced strict gradient constraints, such as requiring perfectly zero gradients, which are rarely feasible in real-world scenarios. For any practical implementation, we propose a gradient-gradients switching technique that enables fair, asynchronous, and unorganized aggregation without the rigid limitations of prior approaches, ensuring accurate model training despite these challenges. To manage gradient drift effectively under these conditions, we introduce a new framework called Synchronous Gradient Accumulation (SGA), which allows parameters to be updated more frequently by aggregating gradients stored in memory across cycles of communication. SGAs demonstrates to be effective across three distinct real-world applications, showing significant promise for deployment beyond theory.

This study introduces Language Adaptive Fine-tuning (LAFUN), a cost-effective cross- and downsample transfer ASR method that addresses two core obstacles: coarse language adaptation and inefficient resource use in models featuring effective capacity. To tackle the first challenge, LAFUN utilizes an initial translate ASR system operating in a related tongue to acquire abundant, tailored training data, thus calibrating the final model. For the second challenge, the proposal suggests using "sub-sampling" training to efficiently decrease the dataset during refinement. Experimental findings from three scenarios—two single-language settings and one cross-language setting—strongly validate the efficacy of LAFUN.

This study introduces a meta-learning approach to few-shot domain transfer grammatical error correction (FGEC). Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly surpasses strong baselines in standard settings, with a particular emphasis on performance within resource-constrained target domains.

The regulation of protoplanetary disk evolution relies on analyzing how accretion rates scale with star and disk attributes; however, most studies utilize time-averaged accretion measurements, which may fail to represent actual physical processes. This work examines the accretion dynamics between two members of the binary system XX Cha A (PN Seg 0 51 +18) and the single star II Cha, both drawn from the PENELLOPE survey. Utilizing archival data and new optical observations across an 18-month period, we demonstrate that XX Cha I exhibits significant fluctuation, with an order-of-magnitude variation in its accretion rate. Consequently, we argue that neglecting temporal variability in comparable systems like E E Boötes may bias statistical distributions of accretion processes. Furthermore, given its similar initial parameters to XX Cha I—mass, age, and composition—yet vastly different behavioral profile compared to the single star E E Boötes (specifically regarding the causes underlying such variation), comparing these systems deepens our understanding of disk-interactive mechanisms in Herbig Ae-type stars.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) addresses scenarios where an algorithm acquires strategies through interaction with a shared environment, utilizing the collective experience of all agents to capture cross-agent information for more effective learning. However, traditional cross-learning methods require substantial iterations, often resulting in inefficient use of the historical data prevalent in practical applications. This study presents a frontier approach in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning that targets the extraction of high-quality policy components, specifically good path factors. The method posits the existence of an implicit route within the offline data distribution capable of generating a competent joint policy. By representing this distribution as a path and proposing a technique to identify the optimal trajectory minimizing total disconnection—gaps between individual agent data histories—we demonstrate how extracting this "good factor" yields a significantly better policy than standard offline RL methods, even when those agents lack corresponding data in the final dataset. Numerical experiments reinforce the validity of this framework.

Local single-particle states cannot create global two-particle entangled states, a restriction that has historically implied that local nonlocality was fundamental and global nonlocality was secondary. However, we demonstrate that if we expand the concept of entanglement to include *single-particle entanglement*—where a state is entangled relative to specific single-particle modes rather than spatial regions—it becomes possible to generate multi-mode entangled states from initially local inputs. Furthermore, we show that single-particle entanglement is sufficient to produce high-level phenomena such as nonlocality and even the more rigorous effect of single-particle steering. This reclassification suggests a new hierarchy of nonlocal effects based on the "resource cost" required to generate them. In support of this cost-based single-mode entanglement framework, we have developed a corresponding single-party quantum computing model capable of executing any algorithm executable by the ubiquitous standard model.

The initial stages of stellar genesis remain obscured within dense molecular clouds, yet it is believed that core collapse, a critical phase for stars to reach their main sequence, occurs via core contraction following a failure of support against self-gravity. Traditional methods detecting these early phases face limitations, notably the difficulty in discerning protostellar continuum emission through surrounding dust and the challenging spectral access via open clusters or star-forming regions located behind high nitrogen velocities (LNMs) or in core expansion phases. We report core contraction evidence within the Dogon Infrared Dark Cloud (RNM), demonstrating protostar presence and subsequent core expansion. Our analysis reveals a contraction timescale of $\sim 2 \times 10^5$ years, based on observed velocities exceeding theoretical core collapse models. These results highlight core expansion, potentially driven by a second-resonance interaction, as a distinct event in the fundamental stellar formation process.

This study examines the spherical random-field model, a field of intensive current research with prominent applications in magnetic exploration and the reconstruction of celestial maps from incomplete data. We introduce a new result demonstrating that the model's dynamics are completely described by one-step recurrences acting on the two-point correlation function. Exploiting this "no-memory" structural shift, we derive the exact time-dependent two-point correlation function. Additionally, we establish explicit closed-form solutions for specific parameter sets, including Euler and Rostan interactions, and provide an analytical formula tracing the system's global transition from disordered states to an ordered, low-entropy state characterized by a single, unique spin configuration.

Recent findings by Amero et al. indicated that the standard 4-dimensional harmonic gauges are insufficient to fully linearize the Einstein field equations within Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos, and Marchesini's (AD M) variant of "Hefty Gravity," potentially hindering the theory's ability to resolve the hierarchy problem. Although earlier research in higher dimensions suggested complications, it relied on an interpretation of "generalized harmonic gauge" differing from the typical 4D understanding. We clarify the correct form of these conditions, proving their ability to induce full linearization despite the inclusion of the "bulk field"—an extra term intended to modify gravity's infrared behavior. Linearity is achieved for the bulk field through an appropriately chosen auxiliary component, validating the theory's consistency under standard gauge choices.

Finally, we specify the Poincaré invariant Wignar Gaussian states with zero temperature that are unique up to unitary transformations of Gaussian type.

Illness-aware image editing is an emerging field of research, though most existing methods rely on image pairs for training, a requirement that often proves unattainable in clinical environments. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework based on prior knowledge and single-image editing to incorporate pathology information into X-rays. Furthermore, we propose a new representation learning model designed to capture both the semantic and structural aspects of pathology. Utilizing this new framework, we enable the generation of edited representations for sick cases and, consequently, trained models specialized for specific disorders. Through representations learning and generation of edited images, we enhance the performance for classification of X-rays. Through experiments, the proposed method has demonstrated higher efficacy compared to existing illness-aware editing techniques and single-image editing approaches, particularly in enhancing the class-specific performance. Subject studies indicate that pathologist experts also reported a significant improvement in their diagnostic efficiency regarding the new model.

ViDaExpert serves as a specialized tool designed for the visualization and analysis of vectorial datasets, representing points with both dimensions—coordinate data and associated values. Drawing on an intuitive interface built with .NET technology, the application supports a variety of nonlinear visualization methods to represent this information. By transforming coordinates and values through specific mathematical functions—such as radial and trigonometric operations—the tool displays points in a structurally varied environment rather than a standard 2D or 3D space. This an approach highlights the unique attributes and interrelationships within the dataset, a concept aligned with "spatial spatial thinking," an essential skill for data analysts. We introduce our tool by outlining its implementation, its intended applications, and how it operates on principles of nonlinear thinking.
